# Budgeting

A budget is a plan for money before it is spent. Its purpose is not restriction
but visibility: deciding where money should go in advance, rather than
discovering afterwards where it went.

## The 50/30/20 rule

The 50/30/20 rule splits take-home income into three parts:

- **50% needs.** Housing, utilities, groceries, transport to work, insurance,
  minimum debt repayments. Things that continue whether or not you want them to.
- **30% wants.** Eating out, shopping, subscriptions, entertainment, travel.
  Spending that improves life but could be paused.
- **20% savings and debt repayment.** Building an emergency fund, investing,
  and paying down debt faster than the minimum.

It is popular because it is easy to remember and needs no categories beyond
three. It is a starting point, not a law. In cities with high rent, needs alone
can exceed 50%, and forcing the split can mean pretending an essential cost is
optional. The useful discipline is protecting the 20% first, then letting needs
and wants divide what remains.

A common mistake is applying the percentages to gross salary. They apply to
take-home pay, after tax and mandatory deductions.

## Zero-based budgeting

Every unit of income is assigned a job until nothing is unallocated: income
minus all allocations equals zero. Savings and investments are allocations, not
leftovers. This is more work than 50/30/20 but eliminates the vague surplus that
tends to be spent by default.

## Envelope budgeting

Each category gets a fixed allowance for the month. When the allowance is spent,
spending in that category stops until the next month. Originally literal cash in
envelopes, now usually separate accounts or app categories. Effective for
categories with many small discretionary purchases, where a total is easy to
lose track of.

## Paying yourself first

Savings are transferred out on payday, before discretionary spending begins,
rather than being whatever survives the month. This reverses the usual order and
is one of the most reliable ways to raise a savings rate, because it removes the
need for month-long willpower.

## Building a budget from history

A budget invented from nothing usually fails, because it reflects intention
rather than behaviour. A more durable approach starts from what actually
happened over recent months:

1. Total each category over the last three to six months.
2. Take the **median** rather than the average. One unusual month drags an
   average upward, and budgeting to that inflated figure defeats the purpose.
3. Fund essentials at that level, since they are largely fixed.
4. Set a savings target before allocating discretionary spending.
5. Fit discretionary categories into what remains.

Fixed costs such as rent need no headroom — they are the same every month, and
padding them just hides money that could be saved.

## Why budgets fail

- Built on gross rather than take-home income.
- No allowance for irregular annual costs like insurance premiums.
- Too many categories to track.
- No buffer, so a single unexpected expense makes the whole plan void.
- Treating savings as a remainder rather than an allocation.

# Credit and credit scores

Credit is borrowed money that must be repaid, usually with interest. How it is
managed is recorded and affects the cost and availability of future borrowing.

## Credit utilisation

Credit utilisation is the share of available credit currently in use:

utilisation = balance owed / total credit limit

A card with a 100,000 limit carrying a 30,000 balance is at 30% utilisation.

Keeping utilisation **below 30%** is the usual guidance, and lower is generally
better. High utilisation suggests dependence on borrowing, and it is one of the
larger factors in most scoring models.

Two details are easy to miss. Utilisation is normally measured on the statement
date, not at month end — so a balance cleared after the statement is generated
can still be reported as high. And it is assessed both per card and across all
cards combined.

## Credit scores

A credit score summarises borrowing history into a single number, typically
between 300 and 900 in India, and lenders use it to price and approve credit.
The main inputs, roughly in order of weight:

- **Payment history.** Whether past dues were paid on time. The single largest
  factor. One missed payment can affect a score for years.
- **Credit utilisation.** As above.
- **Age of credit history.** Longer histories are viewed more favourably, which
  is why closing an old card can lower a score.
- **Credit mix.** Some variety across secured and unsecured credit.
- **Recent enquiries.** Several applications in a short period suggest
  difficulty obtaining credit.

## Paying in full versus the minimum

Paying a credit card in full by the due date usually incurs no interest. Paying
only the minimum — often around 5% of the balance — is expensive: card interest
is typically in the region of 30-45% a year, and the interest-free period is
usually lost on new purchases until the balance is cleared entirely.

Minimum payments are structured so that a balance can persist for years while
most of each payment goes to interest rather than principal.

## Common misunderstandings

- **Checking your own score does not lower it.** Your own check is a soft
  enquiry; only a lender's application check is a hard enquiry.
- **Carrying a balance does not build credit.** Paying in full on time builds
  credit. Carrying a balance only creates interest.
- **Closing unused cards is not automatically helpful.** It reduces total
  available credit, which raises utilisation, and can shorten credit history.
- **No credit history is not the same as good credit.** Someone who has never
  borrowed may find it harder to borrow than someone with a modest good record.

# Emergency funds

An emergency fund is money set aside specifically for unexpected expenses:
medical costs, urgent repairs, sudden travel, or a period without income. Its
purpose is to absorb a shock without borrowing at high interest or selling
long-term investments at a bad time.

## What counts as an emergency

An emergency is unexpected, necessary and urgent. A broken boiler qualifies. A
holiday, a phone upgrade or a festival purchase does not, however desirable —
those are planned expenses, and planning for them separately is what keeps the
emergency fund intact.

## How much to hold

The common guideline is **three to six months of essential expenses** — not
three to six months of income, and not of total spending. What matters is the
cost of continuing to live: rent, utilities, food, transport, insurance, minimum
debt payments.

Where within that range depends on how stable income is and how many people
depend on it:

- **Three months** suits stable salaried income, dual-income households, or
  someone with few dependants and marketable skills.
- **Six months or more** suits variable or commission-based income, freelance or
  contract work, a single-income household, or anyone supporting dependants.

Someone spending 40,000 a month on essentials is therefore looking at a target
of roughly 120,000 to 240,000.

## Where to keep it

The fund must be available within a day or two and must not fall in value. That
means a savings account, a sweep-in deposit, or a liquid fund — not equities,
not long-tenure fixed deposits with penalties, and not anything whose value
moves with the market. Accepting a lower return is the point: this money buys
certainty, not growth.

Keeping it in a separate account from day-to-day spending matters more than it
sounds. Money that shares an account with routine spending tends to be spent.

## Building one

Building an emergency fund from zero can feel slow enough to be discouraging.
Two things help. First, set an initial milestone of one month of essentials —
reachable in a few months, and enough to cover most common shocks. Second,
automate a transfer on payday so it does not depend on remembering.

If there is high-interest debt, such as a credit card balance, the usual order
is to build a small buffer of about one month first, then clear that debt, then
return to the full three-to-six-month target. The interest saved outweighs the
interest earned.

## After using it

An emergency fund is meant to be spent when an emergency arrives — using it is
not a failure. Rebuilding it becomes the priority afterwards, ahead of
discretionary spending, until it returns to target.

# Investing basics

Investing means committing money to assets expected to grow over time, accepting
that value can fall in the short term. It is distinct from saving, where the
priority is that the money is intact when needed.

This is general education. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any
specific investment.

## Compound interest

Compound interest is interest earned on both the original amount and on the
interest already accumulated. Growth accelerates, because each period starts
from a larger base.

future value = principal x (1 + rate) ^ periods

10,000 at 8% a year becomes about 21,600 after ten years and about 46,600 after
twenty. The first decade adds around 11,600; the second adds around 25,000 from
the same starting deposit. Nothing changed except elapsed time.

This is why starting early matters more than starting large. Someone investing
5,000 a month from age 25 typically ends up ahead of someone investing 10,000 a
month from age 40, despite contributing less in total.

Compounding works in reverse on debt. Credit card interest compounds against the
borrower with the same mathematics.

## The rule of 72

Dividing 72 by the annual return gives the approximate years to double. At 8%,
roughly nine years. At 12%, roughly six. Useful for quick mental comparison, not
for precision.

## Risk and return

Higher expected returns come with greater variability. That variability is the
cost of the return, not a flaw to be engineered away.

- **Low risk** — savings accounts, fixed deposits, government securities.
  Modest, predictable returns.
- **Moderate risk** — debt funds, balanced funds, corporate bonds.
- **Higher risk** — equities and equity funds. Historically the strongest
  long-term returns, with large short-term falls along the way.

The relevant question is not which is best but which matches the time horizon.
Money needed in two years does not belong in equities, regardless of expected
return, because the horizon offers no time to recover from a fall.

## Diversification

Spreading money across assets that do not move together reduces the impact of
any single one performing badly. Holding ten stocks in the same industry is far
less diversified than it appears, because they tend to fall together.

Diversification reduces the risk specific to one company or sector. It does not
remove market-wide risk.

## Inflation

Inflation erodes purchasing power. At 6% inflation, money held in cash loses
roughly half its real value over twelve years. A savings account paying 3% while
inflation runs at 6% is losing about 3% a year in real terms.

This is the argument for investing money that is not needed soon — and equally
the argument for keeping an emergency fund in cash anyway, because certainty of
value matters more than real return for money that must be available.

## Sequence

A widely used ordering, before investing begins:

1. Cover essential expenses.
2. Build an emergency fund of three to six months of essentials.
3. Clear high-interest debt, particularly credit cards.
4. Then invest with a horizon of five years or more.

Investing while carrying credit card debt at 36% is usually a losing trade: few
investments reliably return more than that, and the debt's cost is certain while
the return is not.

# Loans and debt

A loan is borrowed money repaid over time with interest. The two questions that
matter most are what happens if repayment fails, and how the interest is
calculated.

## Secured versus unsecured

A **secured loan** is backed by an asset — the collateral. Home loans are
secured against the property, vehicle loans against the vehicle, gold loans
against pledged gold. Because the lender can recover the asset on default, risk
is lower and interest rates are correspondingly lower. The consequence of
default is loss of the asset.

An **unsecured loan** has no collateral. Personal loans, credit cards and most
education loans fall here. Approval depends on income and credit history rather
than an asset, so rates are higher. Default does not cost a specific asset but
damages credit standing and can lead to recovery proceedings.

As a rough ordering of cost, from cheapest to most expensive: home loan, then
vehicle loan, then education loan, then personal loan, then credit card
borrowing.

## EMI

An EMI, or equated monthly instalment, is a fixed monthly payment covering both
interest and principal so the loan is fully repaid by the end of its term.

The payment stays constant, but its composition changes. Early instalments are
mostly interest, because interest is charged on a large outstanding balance.
Later instalments are mostly principal. This is why repaying early in the term
saves far more interest than repaying the same amount near the end, and why the
total interest paid over a long loan can be a substantial fraction of the amount
borrowed.

Extending the tenure lowers the monthly payment and raises the total interest —
often considerably. A longer loan is not a cheaper loan.

## Fixed and floating rates

A **fixed rate** stays the same for the term, or an agreed part of it. Payments
are predictable, usually at a slightly higher starting rate.

A **floating rate** moves with a benchmark. Payments can fall, and can equally
rise. Lenders often absorb changes by extending the tenure rather than raising
the EMI, which keeps the monthly figure stable while increasing total interest.

## Debt-to-income

Lenders compare total monthly debt payments with monthly income. A ratio below
about 36%, with housing under roughly 28%, is a common comfort threshold.
Beyond that, borrowing is generally harder and more expensive, and the budget
has little room to absorb a shock.

## Order of repayment

With multiple debts, two approaches are widely used:

- **Avalanche.** Pay the highest interest rate first. Mathematically optimal —
  it minimises total interest paid.
- **Snowball.** Pay the smallest balance first. Costs slightly more overall but
  clears individual debts sooner, which some people find easier to sustain.

Either way, minimum payments continue on everything else. The avalanche saves
more money; the snowball is sometimes more likely to be followed to completion.

## Refinancing

Replacing a loan with a cheaper one can reduce cost, but processing fees,
prepayment penalties and a reset tenure can erase the benefit. The comparison
that matters is total remaining cost under each option, not the interest rate
alone.

# Saving and savings rate

Saving is the gap between income and spending. Everything else — where to put
the money, what return it earns — matters less than the size of that gap,
especially early on.

## Savings rate

The savings rate is the share of take-home income not spent:

savings rate = (income - expenses) / income

Someone earning 60,000 and spending 42,500 has a savings rate of about 29%.

It is a more useful measure than the absolute amount saved, because it adjusts
for income. Rising income with an unchanged savings rate means spending grew in
step — the pattern usually called lifestyle inflation.

## Why the rate matters more than the return

Early on, the amount saved dominates the return earned. Saving an extra 5,000 a
month adds 60,000 a year with certainty, while chasing two extra percentage
points of return on a 200,000 portfolio adds 4,000 and is not guaranteed. Only
once the invested amount is large does return begin to dominate. This is why
advice tends to emphasise the savings rate first and portfolio construction
second.

text:
## Paying yourself first

Transferring savings on payday, before discretionary spending, is more reliable
than saving what remains at month end. It converts a month of daily decisions
into one automated transfer.

## Sinking funds

Not every large expense is an emergency. Insurance premiums, festival spending,
annual subscriptions and travel are predictable — they are simply not monthly.
A sinking fund sets aside a twelfth of the annual cost each month, so the
expense arrives already funded. This is what stops predictable costs from
draining the emergency fund.

An annual premium of 18,000 becomes a monthly allocation of 1,500.

## Where savings go, by time horizon

- **Under a year** — savings account or liquid fund. Capital stability matters
  more than return.
- **One to five years** — fixed deposits, recurring deposits, short-duration
  debt funds. Some return, limited volatility.
- **Over five years** — long-term instruments including equity, where time
  smooths out volatility.

Matching the instrument to when the money is needed matters more than maximising
return. Money required next year does not belong anywhere its value can fall.

text:
## Reducing spending without tracking every rupee

The largest savings usually come from a few recurring decisions rather than many
small ones. Rent, vehicle costs, and subscriptions are decided once and then
repeat automatically every month. Reviewing those few commitments is generally
worth more than scrutinising daily purchases.
